analysis.one_liner: Bans drug companies from paying generic makers to delay cheaper competition.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have banned drug companies from paying rivals to delay cheaper generics, never received a vote in any House committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it unlawful for a brand-name drugmaker to pay a generic or biosimilar competitor to stay out of the market — a practice known as 'pay for delay,' where a brand company settles a patent lawsuit by compensating the cheaper competitor to delay launching. It would give the Federal Trade Commission the power to enforce the ban, impose civil penalties of up to triple the value exchanged, and require drug companies to file complete settlement agreements, including any side deals or oral promises, with antitrust enforcers [S2][S3]. The bill never got a hearing or a vote in either committee it was referred to.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and consumers who pay for prescription drugs, including through insurance premiums, because generic and biosimilar competition is one of the most reliable ways to bring drug prices down; when a brand-name company pays a generic maker to delay entry, consumers keep paying monopoly prices for years longer. The bill would have cut off that practice.

how_it_helps.text: It makes it unlawful for a brand-name drugmaker to give a generic or biosimilar maker anything of value in exchange for delaying research, manufacturing, or sales of the competing drug [S3].

Violators face FTC enforcement, civil penalties of up to triple the value exchanged, and forfeiture of the first generic's 180-day exclusivity period, making pay-for-delay deals a defined legal violation rather than a gray-area antitrust fight [S2][S3].

It closes a disclosure loophole by requiring companies to certify to the FTC and Justice Department that they filed complete settlements, including side deals and oral promises, so regulators can see what was actually promised [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would lose a profitable way to extend their market monopolies past a generic's availability, and generic makers who accept payment to stay off the market, which the bill makes unlawful with civil penalties [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill's exceptions allow brand-name companies to buy a faster generic launch (an 'authorized generic' arrangement) and pay up to $7.5 million in litigation costs, so some value can still change hands in a settlement without violating the ban [S3].

A near-automatic ban on compensation in settlements, rather than case-by-case antitrust review, could block some settlements that would actually speed a generic to market or give consumers an early low-cost option; the FTC can exempt such agreements only by rulemaking, a slower path [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit was real: these pay-for-delay deals can add months or years of monopoly pricing on drugs patients already rely on, and the bill gave the FTC a direct, enforceable ban with meaningful penalties [S2][S3]. The main drawback is that the exceptions in the bill — allowing authorized generics and limited litigation-cost payments — leave some room for settlements that could still slow competition, and critics of a flat ban argue courts should weigh each settlement's pro-competitive effects rather than prohibiting them by rule [S3]. On the whole, for consumers facing high drug prices, the bill's benefits outweighed its risks; the greater cost was that it never even reached a committee vote [S5].

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees, sent to their health and antitrust subcommittees, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 4, 2021 and referred to two committees, Energy and Commerce and Judiciary, which is the standard first step [S5].
In February and March 2021 it was referred to the Health Subcommittee of Energy and Commerce and the Antitrust Subcommittee of Judiciary, where it sat; neither subcommittee advanced it [S5].
No further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died without a vote in either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drugmakers kept the ability to settle patent disputes by paying generic competitors to delay market entry, preserving extended monopoly pricing [S2].

for.name: Bobby L. Rush
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled initial support from eight House members [S3].

for.name: 17 of 213 House Democrats and 1 of 222 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no cosponsor action moved it out of committee [S4].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and its Health Subcommittee held it without a hearing or markup [S5].

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and its Antitrust Subcommittee held it without a hearing or markup [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Democratic — 17 Democratic cosponsors alongside sponsor Bobby Rush, with just one Republican — but the bill never reached a vote, so the parties' positions were never tested on the record [S4].

industries.note: They would lose their ability to pay generic and biosimilar rivals to stay off the market, ending a tool that has kept monopoly prices in place for months or years past a generic's availability [S2][S3].

They could no longer accept payments to delay launching a competing product, but the bill preserves their ability to win settlements allowing early generic entry and keeps their 180-day exclusivity unless they violate the ban [S3].
The FTC would gain exclusive litigation authority over these settlements, a defined civil penalty up to triple the value exchanged, and stronger disclosure filings from drug companies [S3].
